examples: The new product sold out in no time.
The rumor instantly spread throughout the school.
The sky grew dark, and in an instant it started to rain.
The two of them are talking about something in low voices.
Something smells good from the kitchen.
He seems to be troubled about something.

fields.meaning: Cannot keep (…) any longer (urgent situation); cannot just sit idly and …
examples: We don't have time, so we can't wait for the people who are coming late. Let's start right away.
The exam is tomorrow, so I can't be lazing around here having fun.
Some guests are coming tonight, so I can't be playing tennis or anything. I have to go shopping soon.
Our products are selling well now, but we can't afford to be complacent, because new products keep coming out one after another.
We cannot just stand by and watch this situation.
When the ski season starts, I just can't sit still.
fields.explain: Expresses that, because the situation is urgent, one must not continue doing such a thing, or that one wants to take action quickly. Often used with adverbs such as 「のんびり」, 「うかうか」 and 「じっと」. (２６３)

fields.meaning: Cannot help but (…); cannot stop oneself from (…)
examples: Hearing such a sad story, you can't help but cry.
I knew it was better not to say it, but I couldn't help talking about it.
Anyone who sees that movie would probably be moved.
When it comes to my children, I can't help worrying every day.
fields.explain: Follows the negative form of a verb and expresses that one cannot hold something back by willpower and does it naturally. Used with verbs that express human actions or movements of thought and emotion, such as 「泣く」, 「思う」 and 「感動する」. It implies that the speaker regards this as "only natural". In written language it also becomes 「…せずにはいられない」. (３７１)

examples: Whether it's Yamada or Sato, neither can be said to be suited to this job.
Whether it's a dog or a cat, keeping pets is not allowed in this apartment building.
Whether elected or defeated, running in this election was very meaningful.
Whether you go or not, at least get ready just in case.
Win or lose, I want to fight fair and square.
Whether they won or lost, I want to praise them for doing their best.
fields.explain: Takes up two things of the same kind, or two opposing things, and expresses the meaning "in either case".

examples: Camping life in the mountains has no electricity or gas, but the inconvenience is also part of the fun.
Hot weather is a nuisance, but cold weather is just as hard.
Walking on a sunny day is enjoyable. But walking while getting wet in the rain also has its own charm.
Genius though he may be, he too is only human. He has happy times and sad times.
fields.explain: Means "in the same way". As in 1. ～3., it expresses that something is the same as what was stated before. 4. means "he, a genius, is the same as an ordinary person".

fields.meaning: Make use of, make the most of, apply (…) (生かす/活かす)

fields.connection: N + とか（いう）（+ N）/ plain form + とか

examples: On the way to the office, I was reading this novel the whole time.
While I was walking, the words he had said to me wouldn't leave my mind.
I did nothing but sleep during the trip.
I make a point of studying languages during my commute.
fields.explain: Takes a noun or verb expressing movement and is used when the following action or state continues throughout that time. (３４５)

examples: If it's that part, you can buy it for just 1,000 yen.
A job like this will be done in five minutes.
That story should have reached the other party through Mr. Yamada as well.
Company A also has a partnership with Company C through Company B.
According to information that reached the Ministry of Foreign Affairs through the local embassy, the death toll exceeded at least 100
fields.explain:
Means 「…を経由して」. Used to state that information is conveyed or a relationship is formed by way of something. What is conveyed is information, stories, contact and the like; it cannot be used for means of transportation.
*（誤） この列車はマドリッドをつうじてパリまで行く。
*（正） この列車はマドリッド｛を通って／を経由して｝パリまで行く。
!Written-language style. Also said as 「…をとおして」.

fields.name: question word…かとおもったら
fields.connection: [plain form（including a question word）] + かと思ったら
examples: I wondered what you were going to say, and it's that nonsense?
I wondered what you were doing, skipping meals, and it's video games?
He got up from his seat in the middle of the meeting, and when I wondered where he was going, he said he just wanted to look at the sky. That guy's been acting strange lately.
A two-year-old baby is absorbed in doing something. I wondered what it was doing, and it turned out to be smiling and waving at a mirror.
fields.explain: Expresses the speaker wondering about something and paying attention to it. What follows describes an unexpected discovery or a surprising event.

examples: She is about the only one who would grant such an unreasonable request.
He is about the only one who wouldn't complain about being called out in the middle of the night.
Tanaka is about the only one who can solve this difficult problem within the time limit.
Only new employees would get genuinely angry at his jokes.
Children are about the only ones who can complain in front of their parents.
fields.explain:
Emphatic structure: [clause] + のは + [the only target] + ぐらいのものだ。
“ぐらいのものだ” strengthens the nuance of “only… and no one else”, with a slight exaggeration.
Often used in conversation/narration, and also found in descriptive writing.

• Emphasizes an extremely narrow scope: “only … can / it really is …”.
• Nuance of exaggeration/emphasis on the speaker's emotion (may overstate a little).
• Often used to praise/criticize, or to emphasize something special or exceptional.
fields.notes:
• “ぐらいのものだ” > “くらいだ” in degree of emphasis; both are natural.
• Can be used with time/place: こんな景色が見られるのはここぐらいのものだ。
• Often used with special/exceptional topics for a rhetorical effect.
meaning_vi: Only… and nothing else (emphasis: くらいのものだ)
mistakes: Wrong position of のは: ×彼くらいのものだ助けてくれる → correct: 助けてくれるのは彼ぐらいのものだ。
Overuse in formal writing; in reports, use だけだ to be more neutral.
Understanding it as an absolute fact → in fact it has a nuance of exaggeration/personal emphasis.
JLPT N2–N1: Distinguish it from ～しかない (lack of choices) and ～だけだ (neutral).

rows: ～のは N ぐらいのものだ
できるのは<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>くらいのものだ
<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かるのは<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>だけだ
<ruby>頼<rt>たよ</rt></ruby>れるのは<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>くらいしかない

examples: I was half-listening to the radio and before I knew it I had fallen asleep.
I was idly gazing at the sky in the park.
The scent of flowers drifted in from somewhere.
At some point, the number of foreigners in this town increased.
I was walking aimlessly along the road and came out at the sea.
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker has no clear purpose (looking, listening, thinking, strolling…).
The form question word＋ともなく emphasizes that the origin, place or point in time is “unspecified”.
Not used for strongly intentional acts, commands or clear volition.
Often used in descriptive writing, diaries and novels to create a hazy atmosphere.

• Meaning 1 (unconscious action): Describes doing an action idly, unintentionally, without a clear goal. Example: 聞くともなく聞く (listen absentmindedly).
• Meaning 2 (unknown origin/time): Used with question words such as いつ／どこ／誰 to say “no one knows since when/from where/by whom”. Example: どこからともなく (from somewhere unknown).
• Nuance: Written language, neutral; descriptive, sometimes creating a vague, hazy feeling.
• Grammar: Vるともなく can stand alone or be repeated as VるともなくVる; the subject is usually the speaker/the person observed, in a “relaxed” state.
fields.notes:
• The repeated form VるともなくVる balances the rhythm of the sentence and highlights the “absentminded” quality.
• With question words, から/へ are usually used: どこからともなく, どこへともなく.
• Often seen with verbs of perception: 見る, 聞く, 眺める, 考える, 歩く.
meaning_vi: Unintentionally…, without intention
explain: Describes a “relaxed” state: doing something halfheartedly, without concentrating.
Often used with the repeated form to sound more natural in spoken/written language.
Not used when the speaker wants to show a clear goal or give a command/express volition.
examples: 1. ラジオを聞くともなしに聞いていたら、懐かしい曲が流れてきた。
I was half-listening to the radio when a nostalgic song came on.
2. 通勤電車で外を眺めるともなしに眺めていた。
On the commuter train, I was idly gazing outside.
3. 公園を歩くともなしに歩いていたら、友達に会った。
I was wandering aimlessly in the park when I ran into a friend.
4. SNSを見るともなしに見て時間をつぶす。
Killing time idly scrolling through social media.
5. どこからともなしに拍手が起こった。
Applause broke out from somewhere.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Key difference | Short example
～るともなしに | Doing something absentmindedly | Gentle, rich in everyday nuance | 外（そと）を 眺（なが）めるともなしに …
～るともなく | Doing something absentmindedly; question word＋ともなく is common | Wide use; many set phrases with question words | どこ からともなく …
～ながら | Doing A while doing B | Expresses simultaneity, does not emphasize “absentmindedness” | 音楽（おんがく）を聞（きき）き ながら 勉強（べんきょう）する
～つい | Doing by mistake, unintentionally | Expresses “slipping”/carelessness, unlike prolonged idleness | つい 食（た）べ過（す）ぎた
common_mistakes: • Using it with a command/volition: × 見るともなしに見てください → unnatural.
• Using it for a clear purpose: × 情報を集めるともなしに集める (this action usually has a goal).
• Confusing it with ～つい: ～ともなしに is a prolonged idle state; ～つい is a momentary “slip”.
meaning_vi: Idly…, without intention… (ともなく/ともなしに)
mistakes: Using it for an action with a clear goal: incorrect. Incorrect example: × 目的地へ行くともなく行く (use どこへともなく for going aimlessly).
Confusing it with ～がてら/～ついでに: ～ともなく is unconscious; the other two patterns are intentional.
Dropping から/へ in a phrase with a question word: どこともなく (has a different meaning, “anywhere”); for the meaning “from somewhere unknown” you need どこからともなく.

テレビを<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>るともなく…

fields.connection: どうにか + V (managing to do something): Somehow, finally manage to do it / どうにか + Aい / Na / Adv (just enough degree): A state of just getting by, so-so / どうにかなる: Everything will be fine, it will work out
examples: I somehow made it in time for the last train.
I'm somehow getting by on a small salary.
I want to solve this problem somehow.

fields.meaning: On the premise of…, on the assumption that…
examples: We are dating with a view to marriage.
This plan was made on the assumption that everyone will participate.
We drew up the budget on the premise of a price increase.

fields.meaning: Before…; not even at the level of… (それ以前の問題)
examples: That's a problem that comes before manners.
Before even talking about ability, the problem is that you don't come to practice in the first place.
Before computers became widespread, letters were the main means.

fields.meaning: The situation is that…, that is how… (formal explanation)
fields.connection: V plain form + 次第です
examples: The reason my report was late is that the confirmation took time.
I am contacting you because I would like to ask for everyone's cooperation.
Due to the circumstances described above, we are holding today's meeting.

fields.meaning: At the same time… / While at it…
examples: I have come today to offer my New Year's greetings as well.
I would like to express my thanks and, at the same time, report the results.
Along with sending the materials, I would like to update you on recent developments.
I have come to see the facility and to pay my respects as well.
I visited to offer my apologies as well.
fields.explain:
Formal, polite; suitable for company documents, invitations and speeches.
Often used with keigo: 伺う, 参る, 申し上げる, 拝見する, 致します.
Used for actions such as moving/visiting/exchanging that have a social, courtesy character.

• Meaning: “while at it, at the same time with the purpose N”, in a ceremonial, very polite way of speaking.
• Context: letters, speeches, formal announcements; when visiting someone politely.
• The subject is usually the speaker/the speaker's group. Rarely used to talk about a distant third party.
• The preceding noun is usually a courtesy noun: ご挨拶, お礼, お詫び, ご報告, ご連絡, 見学.
fields.notes:
• Place an N with a “polite purpose” in front to show good manners and a legitimate reason for the visit/contact.
• Effective in business emails: 「ご報告かたがた資料を送付いたします」。
• Avoid overusing it in everyday conversation so as not to sound overly stiff.
mistakes: Using it with casual verbs, without keigo: unnatural in the style of 「かたがた」.
Using it to talk about a distant third party: not typical; keep the speaker as the agent.
Confusing it with 「がてら」: 「かたがた」 is formal and social; 「がてら」 is everyday.
Attaching it to an unsuitable N (an everyday N): something like 「ゲームかたがた」 sounds odd.

rows: Courtesy N; mainly the speaker; keigo verbs
ご<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>かたがた<ruby>伺<rt>うかがう</rt></ruby>う
Going out, doing A and B while at it

fields.connection: V plain form + (か)と思いきや / N + (だ) / Na + (だ) / Aい
examples: Just when I thought the rain had stopped, it started again right away.
I thought today would be easy, but it was actually busy.
I thought it was a price cut, but in fact the contents had been reduced.
Everyone thought he had won, but he was overtaken at the very end.
Just when I thought it would be quiet, construction next door started.
fields.explain:
A formal/lightly humorous style in narration; suitable for headlines: 順調かと思いきや… .
Not used when Y is not contrary but just a normal sequence.
X can be a subjective feeling or an objective sign; Y negates that expectation.

～かと思いきや expresses “I thought/assumed … but (in reality) …”, emphasizing a contrast with a prediction or initial sign. Written-language nuance, newspaper headlines, storytelling.
• X is usually the basis for the prediction; Y is the contrary, surprising result.
• Not used for the speaker's intentional actions such as commands/intentions.
• Often used with adverbials of time/context: ところが・しかし.
fields.notes:
• “きや” in 思いきや is a fixed form; 思う is not conjugated here.
• Often used with Vた to suggest “just when I thought…”.
• Rhetorical effect: creates a “twist” in the story; suitable for essays and leading into newspaper articles.
mistakes: Using it for an ordinary time relation → incorrect; this pattern requires a “contrary result”.
Dropping である before nouns/na-adjectives: you must say N/na + である + かと思いきや.
Attaching a request/command after ～かと思いきや is unnatural on the JLPT.

rows: <ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いきや<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>いた
～かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと／～かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>えば
<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>るかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うとやむ

<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>ったらまた<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>た
Only states the expectation, does not necessarily state a contrary result
<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>った

examples: It may be old, but its performance is sufficient.
It may be inconvenient, but home is where you make it.
There is some risk, but it is worth trying.
He may have his faults, but his sincerity is genuine.
The initial cost may be high, but in the long run it is cheaper.
There are hardships, but you learn a lot.
fields.explain:
Style of speeches/reports/light academic writing; polite, formal.
The first clause is usually short and concise; the second clause develops the main argument.
Suitable when you want to “acknowledge a drawback but still be supportive”.

• A formal concession structure: admits a shortcoming/disadvantage, but affirms the latter part.
• Typically used with nouns of quality (古さ/不便さ/欠点/リスク/難点/苦労).
• Focuses emphasis on the second clause, usually expressing a positive evaluation/affirmation.
fields.notes:
• こそ creates strong emphasis; あれ is a verb form of ある (classical continuative form) giving a written-language nuance.
• Nominalization of adjectives with 〜さ makes it natural: 高さこそあれ／弱さこそあれ.
• Often used with quantifiers 多少の／わずかな to play down the shortcoming.
mistakes: Using it directly with verbs or adjectives that are not nominalized: ×高いこそあれ → ○高さこそあれ.
The second clause must not totally negate the topic: “古さこそあれ、全然価値がない” clashes in style; use ものの instead.
JLPT: recognize the formal flavor and the combination limits (N/〜さ) to choose こそあれ correctly.

rows: <ruby>古<rt>ふる</rt></ruby>さこそあれ<ruby>快適<rt>かいてき</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いものの<ruby>満足<rt>まんぞく</rt></ruby>。
Even though it is said… still…
Used in both conversation and writing; flexible.
<ruby>不便<rt>ふべん</rt></ruby>とはいえ<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>める。
Used with Vます/いA/なA; quite colloquial.
<ruby>小<rt>ちい</rt></ruby>さいながら<ruby>機能<rt>きのう</rt></ruby><ruby>的<rt>てき</rt></ruby>。

fields.connection: N + こそすれ + [second clause] / Vます
examples: I may have doubts, but I cannot agree.
One may have doubts about his sincerity, but there is nothing to criticize.
As time passes, affection only deepens; it never fades.
The new system may cause confusion at first, but it is not something that leads to chaos.
We would praise effort, but never make fun of it.
fields.explain:
Form: with verbs, use Vます without ます + こそすれ; with nouns, use N + こそすれ directly.
Semantic link: the second clause is usually followed by ～ない／～はしない／～できない／～ことはない to clearly negate.
Nuance: formal, decisive, “closing off the proposition”; suitable for written language, speeches and serious commentary.
Pragmatics: emphasizes the “upper limit” of A (the most that can be admitted) and denies any other interpretation.

～こそすれ emphasizes one-sidedness: it admits possibility/phenomenon A while firmly rejecting possibility B. It can be understood as: “if anything, only A, and absolutely not B.”
• Strong degree of affirmation/negation, with a formal, argumentative flavor.
• Often used to counter the listener's or public's prediction: “You think B? No. At most it's A.”
• The second clause takes a negative: ～ない／～はしない／～できない… to close off the meaning completely.
fields.notes:
• こそ here is a strongly emphatic particle, giving a literary tone when combined with すれ (the continuative form of する in its classical form).
• Part A is usually the “highest/furthest” thing the speaker is willing to admit; part B is the remaining possibilities, which are negated.
• Often used with abstract nouns or mental actions: 疑問・不満・期待・評価・尊敬・戸惑い…
mistakes: Wrong form: with verbs, use the Vます form (without ます); do not use the dictionary form directly.
Missing negation in the second clause: the pattern requires the relation “only A, not B”, so a clear negative marker is needed.
Confusing it with ～こそあれ: both are formal, but こそすれ negates B; こそあれ means “although A, (still) B”.
Nuance: used in a serious style; in casual speech it can sound “stiff”.

rows: Strongly negates B; written language, decisive
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れこそすれ、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>はしない。
Concedes A (usually negative) but result B still holds
<ruby>不便<rt>ふべん</rt></ruby>こそあれ、<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>みやすい。
Softer, without the “only A, not B” constraint
<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>とはいえ<ruby>油断<rt>ゆだん</rt></ruby>できない。
It is said to be A, but actually B
